overview: This section introduces Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) as AWS's Infrastructure as a Service offering: the ability to rent virtual machines and combine them with EBS drives, ELB load distribution and Auto Scaling Groups. It then lists the launch-time sizing and configuration choices (OS, CPU, RAM, storage type, network card, security group, User Data) and explains EC2 User Data bootstrapping. The exam tests EC2 constantly, especially instance family/size selection, security groups as stateful virtual firewalls, and the "runs once, as root, at first boot" rule for User Data.

coreConcepts.definition: AWS Infrastructure as a Service offering whose main capability is renting virtual machines in the cloud.
The cloud model EC2 represents: you rent raw compute (VMs), storage and networking and manage the OS and everything above it yourself.
Network-attached virtual drives used to store data for EC2 instances.
Service that distributes incoming load/traffic across multiple machines.
Service that scales the number of EC2 instances automatically to match demand.
The launch-time choices: OS (Linux, Windows or Mac OS), compute power & cores (CPU), RAM, storage, network card speed and public IP, firewall rules and bootstrap script.
Storage accessed over the network and separate from the host: EBS and EFS are the two named examples.
Storage physically attached to the host machine the instance runs on, as opposed to network-attached EBS/EFS.
The firewall rules attached to an instance; it is configured as one of the EC2 launch options.
A bootstrap script supplied at launch that runs commands automatically when the instance first starts.
Launching commands automatically when a machine starts, so the instance configures itself without manual login.

mustRemember: EC2 = Elastic Compute Cloud = Infrastructure as a Service.
The four main EC2 capabilities: rent virtual machines (EC2), store data on virtual drives (EBS), distribute load across machines (ELB), scale services with an Auto Scaling Group (ASG).
OS choices at launch: Linux, Windows or Mac OS.
Storage choices split into network-attached (EBS & EFS) and hardware (EC2 Instance Store).
Other launch options: amount of CPU/cores, amount of RAM, network card speed and Public IP address, security group firewall rules, and the EC2 User Data bootstrap script.
EC2 User Data runs ONLY ONCE, at the instance's first start.
The EC2 User Data script runs with the root user.
Typical User Data tasks: installing updates, installing software, downloading common files from the internet — anything you can script.

keyComparisons.difference: Network-attached storage is separate from the host and reached over the network; Instance Store is hardware storage tied to the physical machine.
EC2 rents the virtual machine, EBS stores its data on virtual drives, ELB distributes load across machines, ASG scales the number of instances.
User Data automates boot tasks at first start with no login needed; it is not a recurring configuration mechanism because it runs only once.
Both are launch-time configuration options, but the security group is the firewall rule set while CPU/RAM define compute capacity.

commonMisunderstandings: User Data does NOT run on every boot or restart — it runs only once, at the instance's first start.
User Data does not run as an unprivileged or default login user — it runs as root.
EC2 is not Platform as a Service: it is Infrastructure as a Service, so you own the OS and above.
Storage at launch is not only EBS: EFS (network-attached) and EC2 Instance Store (hardware) are also options.
ELB and ASG are not part of the instance itself — they are separate services that distribute load and scale the fleet.
mentalModels: Think of EC2 as renting a computer in AWS's data center, with EBS as the drives you plug into it, ELB as the traffic cop in front and ASG as the hand that adds or removes computers.
Think of a security group as the firewall rule set stapled to the instance at launch.
Think of User Data as a first-boot setup script burned into the machine image: it fires once, as root, and never again.
Think of network-attached vs hardware storage as 'drive over the network cable' vs 'disk physically in the box'.
edgeCases: User Data can do 'anything you can think of' via scripting — it is not limited to updates and software installs.
Mac OS is a valid EC2 OS option alongside Linux and Windows.
The network card choice includes both speed of the card and whether there is a Public IP address.
Because User Data runs once, any configuration needed after first boot must be handled another way.
Hands-on scope: launch a Linux instance from the AWS Console, observe the parameters, launch a web server via User Data, and start / stop / terminate the instance.

whenToUse.situation: You need a server that installs updates, installs software or downloads files automatically the first time it boots.
You need persistent data storage for an instance, reachable over the network.
You need storage physically attached to the host.
Traffic must be spread across multiple machines.
The number of instances must scale with the service's load.
You need to control which traffic reaches the instance.

examTraps.trap: Choosing 'the User Data script re-runs on every restart to keep the instance updated'.
examTraps.correction: User Data runs only once, at the instance's first start — not on restarts.

examTraps.trap: Assuming User Data runs as the default login user or requires sudo to install software.
examTraps.correction: The User Data script already runs with the root user.

examTraps.trap: Describing EC2 as a managed/serverless platform where you don't manage the OS.
examTraps.correction: EC2 is Infrastructure as a Service — you configure and own the OS, CPU, RAM, storage and firewall choices.

examTraps.trap: Saying storage options at launch are only EBS.
examTraps.correction: Storage is network-attached (EBS & EFS) or hardware (EC2 Instance Store).
ELB distributes load across machines; ASG scales the services by adjusting instances.

beyondSource: The SAA-C03 exam guide names 'instance types, families, and sizes (for example, memory optimized, compute optimized, virtualization)' and selecting the appropriate instance family/size as exam tasks — expect family-selection scenarios beyond the source's brief sizing list.

Security groups appear in the exam guide under designing VPC architectures with security components (security groups, route tables, network ACLs, NAT gateways); the source defines them only as firewall rules.
EC2 Auto Scaling is listed as an in-scope compute service and AWS Auto Scaling under management and governance — distinguish the EC2 scaling service from the broader AWS Auto Scaling.
The exam guide also lists EC2 purchasing options (Spot, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans) and EC2 hibernation as cost-optimization topics; these are not covered in this section.
